1.4.note: FAO-compiled index; latest available reference year is 2022, series discontinued after 2022 in WDI. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the index to exceed 115. Egypt's published value of 109.1 (2022) falls 5.9 points short of that cut; no source in the retrieved pages reports an Egyptian food production index at or above 115 on the 2014-2016 base. (CEIC reports 124.98 for Egypt in 2016, but that is on the older 2004-2006=100 base and is therefore not comparable to this indicator's cut points, and CEIC is T5.). 1.3.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.3.note: ILO modeled estimate (ILOEST) nowcast for 2025, not a directly observed survey figure; World Bank portal displays the value rounded to whole percent. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the agricultural employment share to have fallen below 15 percent of total employment. It has not: the ILO modeled 2025 value is 18 (17.52 unrounded on the same ILOSTAT series per the T5 aggregator), and the observed CAPMAS 2024 survey figure is higher still at 18.7 percent. Neither the modeled nor the survey-based measure is within three points of the 15 cut, and the series is declining by roughly half a point per year, so no published figure supports the next rung. The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading. The series also covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than agriculture alone — this is the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The reference-year 2025 figure is an ILO MODELLED nowcast rather than an observed labor force survey result. An observed national figure sits alongside it: CAPMAS's 2024 annual labor force survey, as reported by the State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce' — consistent with the modeled 18 and confirming the modeled series is not drifting from national data. A commercial T5 aggregator (statbase.org) reproduces the same ILOSTAT series at 17.52 percent for 2025 and 17.98 for 2024, i.e. the unrounded value behind the World Bank's 18. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (ILO modeled estimate)) reports 17.52 for 2025, which differs from the value recorded here.

1.2.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Cereal yield (kg per hectare), Egypt, Arab Rep. (AG.YLD.CREL.KG)
1.2.note: Next level not proposed: Not required: level 5 is the top rung and the published value of 7402 kg/ha lies above the highest cut point of 6000. The World Bank indicator AG.YLD.CREL.KG is precisely 'Cereal yield (kg per hectare)', sourced from FAO production data (FAOSTAT QCL), national-level, covering wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains harvested for dry grain. 1.1.note: Denominator (agricultural employment) is an ILO modeled estimate; WDI metadata notes 'Data on employment are modeled estimates by the International Labor Organization (ILO) ILOSTAT database.'. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because the published value, 8,942.42 constant 2015 US$, falls short of the 10000 cut point by roughly 1,058 dollars. No source in the retrieved pages publishes an Egypt figure at or above 10000 for this construct on any price basis or any reference year; the Arab World aggregate does exceed 10000 (10,945.1 in 2025) but that is a regional aggregate, not Egypt, and cannot be substituted. Should the definition be ratified as current US$ rather than constant 2015 US$, the level could move, but no current-US$ per-worker figure for Egypt was found in these pages. The indicator name reads 'Agriculture value added per worker (USD)'. The published series actually retrieved is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose long definition covers 'Agriculture, forestry, and fishing ... ISIC (Rev. 4) divisions 01-03' and is denominated in constant 2015 US$, not current USD. So the evidence sits on the broader-scope, constant-price side of the unratified definitional question: sector scope is wider than 'agriculture' alone (it includes forestry and fishing), and the price basis is a 2015 constant-dollar series rather than the bare 'USD' the name implies. Figure is national for Egypt, which is what the indicator asks for. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD): 8942.42 for 2025.

1.5.value: DATA GAP — Started with the T1 CAPMAS pages (Sources 1-5): the annual bulletins on production, foreign trade and availability for consumption define الفاقد (losses during sorting, packing, transport, storage, processing) as a term in the food-balance identity and publish self-sufficiency ratios, per-capita availability and food-gap figures, but the retrieved text contains no loss percentage - dead end for a national rate. Then Source 6 (MDPI Sustainability, wheat value chain, ICARDA/ARC): only quantified Egypt figure found, 20.62% of wheat supply lost or wasted, but scoped to wheat and to loss-plus-waste. Source 7 (ScienceDirect, wheat/water) returned a Cloudflare captcha page with no data. Source 8 (Foods 2017, Kumar & Kalita) is a global developing-country review with no Egypt-specific rate in the retrieved text. Source 9 (COMCEC/NRI presentation, T5) is the only source addressing Egyptian cereal post-harvest losses directly, and it states the literature is limited, gives a 16-48% range from 1970s work, notes APHLIS does not cover North Africa, and applies a 10% guesstimate - a T5 tier that cannot carry a statistic in any case. No FAO Food Loss Index or FAOSTAT loss-percentage page for Egypt was among the supplied sources.
1.5.note: Wheat-only value-chain study combining loss and waste; denominator includes imported wheat. Secondary range figure comes from a conference presentation citing 1970s literature and an explicit 'guesstimate'. Next level not proposed: Nothing in the retrieved pages reports an all-crop, harvest-to-market loss percentage for Egypt separated from consumption-stage waste, and no national statistical office or FAO/FLI country estimate for Egypt appears in the supplied set; without that, even level 1 would rest on a construct the sources do not measure. The indicator name asserts an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate. The best available Egyptian figure (20.62%) is (i) wheat only, not all crops; (ii) loss AND wastage across the full life cycle, so it includes retail and household food waste that falls outside 'post-harvest loss'; and (iii) computed over total supply including imports rather than over domestic harvested production. The COMCEC/NRI case study (T5) states for Egyptian cereals: 'Limited published literature on postharvest losses in Egypt. Literature from 1970's suggests a range of 16-48%' and that the authors 'made a guesstimate' of 10% postharvest loss for wheat, maize and rice - again cereals only, and self-described as a guess. CAPMAS bulletins define a loss term (الفاقد, quantities lost during sorting, packing, transport, storage and processing) inside the food-balance identity but the retrieved pages carry no percentage for it.
1.5.defnote: The name asserts an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate; both countries record cereals-only figures, and Egypt's scored figure is described by its own source as covering pre- AND post-harvest losses.

1.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two T1 official-statistics routes first: FAO Microdata catalog entry for Egypt's 2009-2010 Agricultural Census — scope list covers holdings characteristics, area, irrigation, employment, machinery and livestock, with no marketing or sales-channel item; CAPMAS NADA Agriculture collection (47 studies) and the Annual Bulletin of Cooperative Activity in Agricultural Sector 2016/2017 front matter — the bulletin covers cooperative numbers, members, capital, loans and 'marketing' services by governorate, but the retrieved text is preface/index only with no smallholder market-access rate. 2) Went to the peer-reviewed/analytical tier: Tabe-Ojong & Abay (AgEcon Search PDF) and its RePEc listing — construct is participation in contract farming/high-value chains among irrigated smallholders, no national access percentage in the retrieved text. 3) Checked government artifacts: MALR PRIME project page — outputs only (42 thousand acres of marketing contracts, 256 marketing committees, 7 governorates). 4) Checked grey literature: GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment 2023 (contents list flags 'Market Access' and a 'Selling point' figure for a 100-farmer Minya/Beni Suef sample, values not in retrieved text) and GIZ AIP industrial scan 2022 (qualitative factors affecting inclusive procurement, six governorates, no rate). Dead ends: no FAOSTAT/WDI/RuLIS indicator on formal-market participation surfaced; no national household or farm survey table on channel of sale was among the supplied pages. Concluded found=false with abstain hold.
1.6.note: Next level not proposed: Even the lowest rung (below the 20 cut) is withheld because the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian smallholders with formal-market access — not a low one and not a high one. The specific missing item is a nationally representative survey or official statistic reporting the proportion of Egyptian smallholders selling through formal channels (contracts, cooperatives, registered wholesale/export buyers, organised retail); no such published proportion appears in the supplied material. Indicator name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets, expressed as a percentage. The best available Egyptian evidence in these pages is Tabe-Ojong & Abay (IFPRI), 'Smallholder farmers' participation in profitable value chains and contract farming: Evidence from irrigated agriculture in Egypt', which estimates a multivariate probit of joint PARTICIPATION in value chains and contract farming among a survey sample of irrigated smallholders — participation in one contractual channel is not the same as access to formal markets, and the sample is regional (irrigated governorates), not national. Its only quotable general statement is that participation 'remains low in Africa', which is a continental, not Egyptian, claim. Contextual non-matching material: GIZ AIP industrial scan (T4) describes willingness of buyers to source from smallholders in six Upper Egypt governorates qualitatively with no rate; MALR's PRIME page (T3) reports programme outputs — 'Implementing marketing contracts for 42 thousand acres' and 'Forming 256 marketing committees for the small farmers' in seven governorates — which are project counts, not a share of smallholders with market access; GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment lists a 'Selling point' figure for a 100-farmer Minya/Beni Suef sample, again neither national nor a published access percentage. None of these can substitute for the named construct.
1.6.defnote: The name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets; Egypt records a regional contract-farming PARTICIPATION rate from seven governorates and Nigeria a 2012/13 channel-of-sale share — two different constructs, neither of which is access, and neither national in Egypt's case.

1.7.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. (1) CAPMAS censusinfo bulletin on investment loans to farmers — read fully; it reports totals in billion pounds by loan maturity, with the extracted text's digits largely stripped; no farmer counts or percentages. (2) and (3) CAPMAS Annual Bulletin of agricultural sector cooperative activity 2016/17 and 2017/18 — read prefaces and full table indexes; every loan table is 'value of in-kind and in cash loans granted ... and the benefitted areas', i.e. money and feddans by governorate, plus association membership counts; no table promises borrowers as a share of farmers. (4) CAPMAS agriculture subject landing page — navigation shell only, no data. (5) CAPMAS Zemam and agricultural ownership bulletin overview — land area and ownership metadata, no credit variable. (6) FAO World Census of Agriculture, Egypt 1999/2000 — checked for a credit or 'holdings reporting credit' block; the extract covers holdings, tenure, employment, land use, crops, livestock and machinery, but contains no credit item; noted the 4,541,884 holdings figure only as a potential denominator. (7) ScienceDirect 'Agricultural credit constraints in smallholder farming' — blocked by captcha, nothing readable, dead end. (8) and (9) Ministry of Environment CLEI green-finance pages for the Agricultural Bank of Egypt (English and Arabic) — full product catalog with amounts, tenors and interest rates; supply-side terms only, no uptake or coverage share. (10) Forbes Middle East on Egypt's farm credit — T5, reports CAPMAS investment-loan totals of EGP 56 billion for FY2023-24; useful context but a T5 page may not carry a statistic and in any case reports value, not farmer share. Searched all pages for the words 'percent', '%', 'share of farmers' and 'access to credit' in the credit context; the only percentages present are interest rates, financing ratios (80%, 25-70% of production costs) and year-on-year growth rates. Conclusion: the named construct is not published in any supplied page for Egypt.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: No level, including level 1, is supported: the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian farmers with agricultural credit access, only loan values, loan product terms, and benefitted cultivated area. Level 1 would require a published figure below 10 percent for the named construct, and no such figure appears in the supplied pages. The indicator names a SHARE OF FARMERS with credit ACCESS. The best Egypt evidence in the supplied pages is (a) CAPMAS annual bulletins of agricultural cooperative activity, which tabulate the VALUE of in-kind and cash loans granted by season and governorate and the benefitted AREA (feddans), not the number or share of farmers served; (b) Forbes Middle East reporting CAPMAS figures that investment loans to farmers and agribusiness rose to EGP 56 billion in FY2023-24 — again a monetary total; (c) a Ministry of Environment green-finance page listing Agricultural Bank of Egypt product terms (e.g. crop loans of EGP 2,000–10,000 for small farmers), which describes supply-side offer, not uptake or coverage. Separately, the census note for this row flags that Egypt's previously recorded figure came from Findex-style 'rural adults aged 15+' borrowing, which is both a different population (includes non-farmers) and a different concept (borrowing/use rather than access); no such Findex page was supplied here either, so it cannot be quote-verified. The FAO World Census of Agriculture page for Egypt 1999/2000 gives 4,541,884 holdings, which would be a plausible denominator but the supplied pages contain no matching count of credit-receiving farmers, so no ratio can be formed.
1.7.defnote: The name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS; Egypt records rural adults aged 15+ (a population that includes non-farmers) and Nigeria records smallholder households, and both measure borrowing/use rather than access.

1.8.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order. FAO SHARP+ project page (T1): only a forward-looking target of 8,000 farmers by 2027, no adoption share. FAO family-farming page: blocked by Cloudflare, no content. Scientific Reports / PMC mirror of Swelam et al. 2026 (seven governorates, 2953 farmers): abstract and introduction only in the retrieved text; qualitative 'limited uptake', no adoption percentage in the supplied portion. FAO Knowledge Repository record for 'Toward climate-smart agriculture in Egypt' (2022): catalog record and synopsis only — practice case studies, no adoption statistic on the page supplied (the 92-page PDF itself was not retrieved). Kassem et al. 2019 (Delta Nile, 792 farmers): gives 51.9% with no knowledge of climate change — awareness, not practice adoption, and only two governorates. ICARDA/AFESD raised-bed report: table of contents lists wheat area under mechanised raised beds in Sharkia, but the retrieved text contains only table titles and the executive summary, no percentage values. ScienceDirect item: captcha wall, no content. Exa library page (T5): abstract of an economic analysis with emissions shares, no adoption rate, and tier-5 material cannot carry a statistic in any case. Dead ends: two of nine pages were access-blocked; no FAOSTAT, CAPMAS, Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, or World Bank indicator page carrying a farmer-level CSA adoption share for Egypt was among the supplied sources.
1.8.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing item is any nationally scoped, farmer-denominated adoption rate for a defined set of climate-smart practices in Egypt, from a statistical office, FAO/World Bank database, or nationally representative survey. Closest evidence: (a) Kassem et al. 2019 (Sustainability, via DigitalCommons@USU) surveyed 792 farmers in two Nile Delta governorates and reports that 51.9% had NO knowledge of the climate change phenomenon, with manure use, changed crop patterns and crop rotation the commonest adaptation measures among the aware minority — this is an awareness statistic for two governorates, not a national share of farmers using climate-smart practices; (b) Swelam et al. 2026 (Sci Rep, 2953 farmers, seven governorates) reports qualitatively 'limited uptake of technical adaptation measures' concentrated on 'low-cost, incremental practices' with modern irrigation and digital tools 'rarely adopted' — no adoption percentage is given; (c) the ICARDA/AFESD technical report tabulates the 'Relative Importance of Wheat Areas under MRB Farming in Sharkia Governorate' — a share of AREA under one practice in one governorate, which is the exact land-vs-farmers, single-practice, sub-national mismatch flagged in the indicator census; (d) the FAO SHARP+ project page states a forward-looking target that 'over 8,000 farmers will adopt climate-smart agriculture and biodiversity-friendly practices across 3,000 hectares' by 2027 — a project target, not a denominator-based national share. Egypt has roughly 4-5 million agricultural holders, so 8,000 is not convertible to a meaningful national percentage.
1.8.defnote: The name counts FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices; Egypt records a share of WHEAT AREA under a single practice and Nigeria a share of farmers in two zones adopting at least one climate-resilient crop TRAIT — land, practice-basket and geographic scope all differ from the name.

8.1.src: World Bank Open Data (WDI), Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population) — Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
8.1.note: FAO model-based estimate derived from food balance sheets and household consumption distributions; World Bank portal displays the figure rounded to whole percent (the underlying FAO series value for 2023 is reported elsewhere as 9.4). Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require a prevalence below 7.5 percent. Egypt's published 2023 value is 9 (9.4 in the finer-grained FAO series shown on TheGlobalEconomy's reproduction), which is above 7.5, and the series on the World Bank page is rising rather than falling toward that cut (the y-axis on the Egypt chart runs to 10.0 and the most recent value is the series maximum). Nothing in the supplied pages shows an Egyptian PoU figure under 7.5 for any recent year. The World Bank series SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS is FAO's SDG indicator 2.1.1, prevalence of undernourishment as a percentage of the national population — exactly the named construct, for Egypt, Arab Rep. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 9.4 for 2023, which differs from the value recorded here.
8.1.tier_detail: FAO model-based estimate derived from food balance sheets and household consumption distributions; World Bank portal displays the figure rounded to whole percent (the underlying FAO series value for 2023 is reported elsewhere as 9.4)

8.5.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. Source 1 and Source 2 (CAPMAS censusinfo, T1, Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 and 2015): catalog landing pages listing downloadable press releases, a bulletin and tables, but the retrieved text contains no sex-disaggregated ownership values - the underlying PDFs were not supplied. Source 4 (CAPMAS Arabic 'zemam and agricultural ownership' bulletin overview, T1): abstract and keywords cover total zemam, government and private lands and 'المساحة المملوكة' (owned area), but the unit of analysis is stated as feddans and no gender breakdown appears; this is the most likely home for an Egyptian owner-based figure and is the gap to close on a rerun. Source 3 (FAO microdata, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010, T1): methodology metadata only; scope lists holding characteristics and employment, no published results table. Source 5 (FAO Gender and Land Rights Database, T1): the deep link returned a 404 error page, so the GLRD Egypt country profile - the natural custodian for this indicator - could not be read. Source 6 (FAOSTAT structural data from agricultural censuses, T1): confirms the domain disseminates 'sex of agricultural holders' as a percentage of holdings, but the catalog page itself carries no Egypt value; the actual data download was not fetched. Source 7 (FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming in Egypt, T2): the retrieved text stops at the table of contents, which lists '1.2.6 Gender composition of the holders' on page 20 - the figure is very likely there but is not in the text supplied, so quoting it would be fabrication. Source 8 (FAO Country Gender Assessment of the Agriculture and Rural Sector: Egypt, T2): retrieved text is front matter plus the opening of 'Main findings', all qualitative on invisibility and structural barriers; no land-ownership percentage in the supplied extract. Source 9 (GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment, T4): the list of figures includes 'Figure 2: Land ownership by gender', but this is a 100-farmer purposive sample in Minya and Beni Suef, i.e. sub-national and non-representative even if the numbers had been supplied, which they were not. Source 10 (GLTN Arab Land Initiative presentation, T5): the only page carrying an actual Egypt number - 212779 female holders, 4 percent - rejected on tier and on the holder-versus-owner construct as set out in construct_note. Dead ends: no SDG 5.a.1 reporting, no Demographic and Health Survey asset-ownership module, and no CAPMAS ownership tabulation by sex appeared among the retrieved pages.
8.5.note: Next level not proposed: No level was proposed at all, so no next rung applies. The specific missing item is a T1-T4 published figure, for Egypt, for the share of land OWNERS (or landholding-title holders) who are women - or, failing that, an admissible-tier restatement of the census holder share that the assessment could ratify as a proxy after resolving the owner-versus-holder definitional question. Context only, not recorded as the cell value: a T5 slide deck ('Women's land rights in Arab countries', GLTN Arab Land Initiative) tabulates FAO World Programme for the Census of Agriculture 2010 results giving Egypt (census 2009/2012) 5401432 total holders, of whom 212779 (4%) are female holders operating 114694 ha (3%) of area. Two problems sit on top of each other. First, tier: the page is T5, which is admissible for existence facts but never for a statistic, so this number cannot be ratified from the evidence supplied. Second, construct: 'holder' is defined on that same page, per Eurostat, as the person on whose account and in whose name the holding is operated and who bears the economic risk - the holder 'can own the holding outright or rent it or be a hereditary long-term leaseholder or a usufructuary or a trustee'. That is operatorship, not ownership. The indicator as NAMED asks for women who OWN land, so the canonical holder statistic sits on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census. A ratified owner-based figure would need to come from a land-ownership or asset-ownership survey (e.g. SDG 5.a.1, or CAPMAS agricultural property/'zemam' ownership tabulations), none of which are present in numeric form in the retrieved pages.
8.5.defnote: The indicator name says women who OWN land while the canonical statistic counts women agricultural holders (operators), who may rent rather than own.

2.4.src: World Bank World Development Indicators — Individuals using the Internet (% of population), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database)
2.4.note: World Bank portal displays the ITU figure rounded to whole percent; underlying ITU estimate may carry decimals. Next level not proposed: Level 5 would require a published figure above 80%. The most recent ITU/World Bank value for Egypt is 75, five points below the 80 cut; the only other national evidence in the supplied pages (MCIT ICT Indicators in Brief, 72.2% internet penetration for 2021/2022) is lower still, and no admissible source in these pages reports Egyptian individual internet use above 80%. The World Bank/ITU series 'Individuals using the Internet (% of population)' is exactly the named construct, national population basis, for Egypt, Arab Rep. Note the national MCIT survey-based figure of 72.2% internet penetration for 2021/2022 (T3, ICT Indicators in Brief, September 2023) is an earlier-year national figure and is consistent in magnitude. 2.1.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU DataHub Egypt country page for 'Population coverage, by mobile network technology' (i=100095) — returns national-only series for at least 2G/3G/LTE/5G; no rural/urban selector in the retrieved page. 2) ITU Facts and Figures 2025 'Mobile network coverage' chapter — contains the urban/rural narrative but only at world, income-group, region, LDC/LLDC/SIDS level; Egypt is not named. 3) ITU Statistics landing page — confirms an urban/rural coverage time series exists but only 'for the world, by geographic regions, by urban/rural area and by level of development', i.e. aggregates, not countries. 4) ITU Measuring Digital Development 2025 and 2023 PDFs and Facts and Figures 2020 PDF — front matter and regional charts only; no Egypt rural coverage value in the retrieved text. 5) ITU estimation-methods document — confirms 'Percentage of the population covered by mobile networks (at least 3G, at least LTE/4G)' is modeled at national level; no rural variant documented. 6) MCIT ICT Indicators in Brief September 2023 and the MCIT Indicators index (T3, the national regulator/ministry) — mobile penetration, mobile Internet users, ADSL by governorate group, and 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas' (fixed, not mobile broadband); no rural mobile broadband coverage figure. 7) nPerf coverage map — T5 crowdsourced, no quotable statistic and inadmissible for a prerequisite row. Dead end on the named construct.
2.1.note: ITU country coverage values are operator-reported/modeled national estimates with no urban-rural disaggregation published at country level. Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is claimed; the specific gap is that no source states what share of Egypt's RURAL population is within range of a 3G or 4G signal. Even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 would also require a rural figure (below 20) that no publisher has produced. The indicator names RURAL coverage. The best available Egypt-specific evidence is NATIONAL: ITU DataHub reports for Egypt, 2025, 'At least 3G 99.8%', 'At least LTE/WiMAX 98%', 'At least 2G 99.9%', 'At least 5G 11%' (% of individuals). These are whole-population figures and cannot be read as rural coverage: ITU's own 2025 Facts and Figures shows that the uncovered residual is 'exclusively rural', so a national figure systematically overstates the rural value by construction. This cell therefore sits on the wrong side of the census's open question: recording the ITU national at-least-3G number here would mechanically score level 5 for a rural construct that no source has measured for Egypt. ITU's global/regional rural numbers (e.g. 4G covering 84 per cent of rural areas worldwide; Arab States 5G 13 per cent) are aggregates, not Egypt values, and rule 5 forbids importing them.
2.1.defnote: The name asserts RURAL coverage, but Egypt's row records the ITU national at-least-3G figure as a clean cls="Measured" number that scores level 5 mechanically, while Nigeria records a rural-but-4G-only modelled estimate — so the register's only universal connectivity prerequisite carries a…

2.5.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU ICT prices landing page (itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/ICTprices) — confirms the 2025 collection, the four baskets and links to country-level 2008-2025 Excel downloads, but carries no country values in text. 2) ITU DataHub IPB dashboard filtered to Egypt (datahub.itu.int and beta.datahub.itu.int, ?e=EGY) — both returned navigation shells plus the indicator picker listing the four baskets; no rendered data. 3) beta.datahub.itu.int/data/?e=EGY&i=100122 ('Current ICT price baskets') — same, only the fixed-broadband basket definition text, no numbers. 4) ITU 'Measuring digital development: The affordability of ICT services 2024' PDF — supplied text stops at the foreword/contents; contains the Broadband Commission 2 %-of-monthly-GNI target language but no Egypt row. 5) ITU ICT Price Basket Statistics Manual 2025 — methodology only, confirms basket definitions and the retirement/legacy status of the 2021-2024 high-consumption definition; no country data. 6) Legacy ITU IPB page (itu.int/ITU-D/ict/ipb) — 2008/2010 composite IPB, wrong construct (composite of fixed telephone, mobile cellular and fixed broadband) and no Egypt figure. 7) World Bank ITIDA ICT indicators report (openknowledge) — indicator-methodology gap analysis for Egypt, no price basket value. 8) Scribd copy of the Egypt Digital Economy Country Assessment — T5 host, only front matter and contents captured, no price figure. Dead end: none of the retrieved pages exposes the Excel/API payload that carries Egypt's basket percentages.
2.5.note: Retrieved pages are client-side-rendered dashboards; the underlying data table did not render into the captured text. Recording either as a national smallholder reach percentage would convert a data gap into a confident figure.

8.11.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) CAPMAS censusinfo household e-indicators 2011 data dictionary — scanned all 229 listed variables for a language field; only 'عدم المعرفة باللغة الإنجليزية' (lack of English knowledge as a barrier to computer use) appears, which is a barrier variable, not a service-language share. (2) CAPMAS ISP survey questionnaire (form A-B) — service-type and coverage questions only, no language-of-service item. (3) CAPMAS ISP variable V45 — the one explicitly language-tagged variable found, 'number of client websites hosted in Arabic'; rejected as a different construct (hosting count, no denominator, commercial web, 2011). (4) CAPMAS Egypt Statistics Journal (Aug 2017) — census/population content, nothing on service languages. (5) OECD e-Government Studies: Egypt 2013 — retrieved text is foreword/acknowledgements; no language-availability statistic surfaced in the supplied extract. (6) Cairo University ICT diffusion paper — macroeconomic and diffusion indicators only; literacy is discussed as a correlate, not service language. (7) MCIT press release on 2025 ICT achievements and the Arabic Digital Egypt strategy page — rich on service counts, users and request volumes, silent on language of delivery. (8) 6Wresearch Egypt Language Services Market — T5 vendor material, narrative only, and inadmissible for a statistic under the tier rules. Dead end throughout: no publisher in the supplied set reports a local-language service share for Egypt.
8.11.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. For any level to be defensible the evidence would need (a) a defined universe of digital agricultural or government services for Egypt, and (b) a count or share of those services available in Arabic or other local languages. Neither exists in the supplied pages; even the highest-quality T1 item (CAPMAS) gives an unnormalised count of Arabic-language hosted websites with no denominator. Indicator names a PERCENTAGE of services available in local languages. The only language-tagged statistic in the supplied pages is CAPMAS's 2011 ISP survey variable 'عدد المواقع المستضافة لصالح العملاء باللغــة العربيـة' (number of client websites hosted in Arabic) — an absolute count of hosted websites from six responding ISPs, not a share of services, not agricultural, and 14+ years old. Contextual figures that are NOT answers to this cell: MCIT reports 210 government services on the Digital Egypt platform in 2025 (up from 170 in 2024) with 10.7 million users, but publishes no language breakdown; the MCIT Digital Egypt strategy page is itself written in Arabic, which is suggestive but is not a published measurement. This cell sits squarely on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question: no Egyptian publisher supplies a denominator for local-language service delivery, so a %-share formulation is currently unmeasurable for Egypt from official sources.
8.11.defnote: Should 8.11 remain a %-share indicator when no country publishes a denominator for local-language service delivery — and the Nigeria bundle's guidance text is contaminated with Egypt-specific content that must be removed regardless of the ruling?

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked UNdata/FAOSTAT 'Cereal import dependency ratio (percent) (3-year average)' (Source 2), the canonical T1 source for this exact indicator \u2014 Egypt is listed as a selectable country but the rendered page text stops at Albania (page 1 of 81 records); no Egypt value present to quote. 2) Checked FAO openknowledge Figure 52 'Cereal import dependency ratio, top countries (2017\u20132019)' (Source 6) \u2014 lists only ~20 top-ranked countries; Egypt not among them. 3) Checked FAO GIEWS Country Brief Egypt (Sources 1 and 3) \u2014 gives cereal import requirements in tonnes and production forecasts, no dependency ratio. 4) Checked USDA FAS Grain and Feed Annual Egypt (Source 8) \u2014 wheat/corn production, consumption and import tonnages only, no ratio. 5) Checked UN Comtrade cereals for Egypt (Source 5) \u2014 trade values/weights only. 6) Checked Springer Food Security Egypt/Jordan paper (Source 7) \u2014 states 50% food import dependence for Egypt, a different construct. 7) Checked CAPMAS metadata catalog entry (Source 4) \u2014 bibliographic record only, no figures. 8) Food Systems Dashboard page (Source 10) blocked by a browser verification checkpoint, no data returned. Conclusion: the figure very likely exists in FAOSTAT's Suite of Food Security Indicators for Egypt, but it is not in the supplied pages, so nothing is recorded.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: Next level not proposed: No level proposed because this is an unscored carried candidate and, separately, no admissible Egypt-specific value for the named construct was quotable from the supplied pages. Nearest available Egypt-specific figures in the retrieved pages measure different constructs: (a) Springer/Food Security (Source 7) states Egypt and Jordan are 'highly dependent on food imports (Egypt 50%, Jordan 95%)' \u2014 this is overall food import dependence, not the FAO cereal import dependency ratio (cereal imports / (production + imports \u2212 exports)); (b) FAO GIEWS (Sources 1 and 3) gives Egypt's 2026/27 cereal import requirement in tonnes (29 million tonnes, of which wheat 13.5 million and maize 15.5 million) \u2014 a volume, not a ratio; (c) UN Comtrade (Source 5) gives cereal trade values and weights, not a dependency ratio. Converting any of these into a percentage would be a derived estimate, not a published figure.

8.17.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata catalog (T1) — central catalog and Agriculture collection pages listed: 47 agriculture studies covering income estimates, prices, animal disease, cooperative activity; no climate-advisory or extension-reach variable surfaced. The one variable-level page retrieved (V3121, 2011 social services bulletin) codes types of agricultural services delivered by local units, not advisory receipt. 2) FAO STI Portal (T1) entry for Egypt's Early Climate Warning app — confirms existence, maturity and target group (Upper Egypt farmers) but its own text states specific adoption rates are not provided. 3) IFAD SAIL supervision report (T1) — lists Early Warning System and CCICRE among acronyms and rates 'Adaptation to Climate Change' 4/6, but the retrieved text carries no advisory-reach figure. 4) WFP Egypt publication page (T1) — gives Upper Egypt livelihood shares (63% of zone employment, ~85% of rural households) but nothing on advisory reach. 5) IFPRI/CGIAR CSA policy seminar note (T2) — richest description of the advisory supply chain (EMA forecasts, CCIC daily warnings, Bashaer, Nabta, FAO regional EWS review) and explicitly flags a communication gap, unquantified. 6) Scientific Reports farmer survey, seven governorates (T2) — measures awareness/adaptation, not advisory receipt. 7) FAO geodata toolkit link returned a 404 page. 8) Sada Elbalad (T5) — expansion of extension and digital advisory services, 7,000+ wheat demonstration fields; existence facts only, ineligible for a statistic. Conclusion: no reach percentage published for Egypt in these pages; hold set.
8.17.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing element is any published numerator/denominator or survey-based share of Egyptian farmers receiving climate or agro-meteorological advisories; the strongest retrieved statement on receipt is qualitative and negative (smallholders often never receive warnings), with no figure attached. The indicator name — 'Climate advisory reach (%)' — reads as farmer-side receipt: the share of farmers/farm households actually reached by climate advisories. Every retrieved Egyptian source sits on the supply side of the census's open question. The IFPRI/CGIAR policy note (T2) describes the Climate Change Information Center issuing daily climate warnings and the Bashaer platform delivering tailored climate-smart recommendations, and explicitly records the opposite of a reach figure — that communication gaps mean many smallholders never receive the warnings — but attaches no percentage to either issuance or receipt. The FAO STI Portal entry (T1) rates the Early Climate Warning app 'Mature'/'Ready' and notes in its own adoption narrative that specific adoption rates are not provided. The Scientific Reports study of 2,953 farmers across seven governorates (T2) reports high climate awareness alongside rare adoption of digital tools, but its abstract as retrieved gives no percentage for advisory receipt, and awareness is in any case a different construct from advisory reach. The news item (T5) cites more than 7,000 wheat demonstration fields — an activity count, not a reach share, and T5 material cannot carry a statistic. CAPMAS catalog pages retrieved contain no climate-advisory variable at all.
8.17.defnote: Does the indicator measure farmer receipt of advisories, or supply-side issuance (warnings issued, platforms live), which is all either country publishes?

8.12.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata catalog (T1): Central Data Catalog, the Agriculture collection (47 studies) and the Annual Bulletin of Agricultural Income Estimates 2013-14 / 2014-15 / 2015-16 / 2016-17 — these are sector income accounts and production statistics, containing no evaluation of any digital tool and no attribution of yield or income change to digitalisation; dead end for this construct. 2) CAPMAS Economic Census 2022/23 and HIECS 2021 access page — household/enterprise statistics, no digital-agriculture impact content. 3) World Bank (T1/T2) 'Accelerating the transformation of Egypt's agri-food system: Impact of investments in selected value-chains' (2021) — the retrieved text is front matter plus table of contents only; it shows a section 5.5 'Digital Technologies' at p.46 within an AIDA-model ex-ante impact analysis, but no page text with a yield or income figure for digital technologies was returned, so nothing could be quoted. 4) CGSpace 'E-Extension and Digital Augmentation of the Egyptian ...' (T2, the most on-point item) — the bitstream URL returned a DSpace login page; no substantive text retrieved. 5) Springer Applied Water Science (T2) drip-irrigation sugarcane field study, Upper Egypt — real yield (+22%) and profit (+50%) outcomes, but the treatment is drip irrigation, not a digital tool; recorded in construct_note as context only. 6) Exa library abstract on extension methodologies in Upper Egypt (T5) — mentions mobile advisory services and yield gains, but T5 is not admissible for a statistic and the abstract attributes the yield figures to non-digital methods. Conclusion: the domain was searched but the two decisive digital documents were unreadable, so the cell is held rather than recorded as Absent or as found.
8.12.note: Nearest digital-specific document (World Bank 2021) is an ex-ante modeled investment analysis (AIDA model), not an ex-post evaluation of realised yield or income change; the CGSpace e-extension study was behind a login wall. Next level not proposed: Not scored: quality_evidence and scale_evidence are both empty because no evaluation, audit or reach figure for a digital-agriculture impact study in Egypt could be quote-verified. Filling either from the drip-irrigation trial would attach an irrigation result to a digital indicator and inflate this row and every mean it enters. The indicator's name fixes the outcome as YIELD or INCOME attributable to digital agriculture. The only retrieved Egypt evidence with hard yield/income outcomes is a peer-reviewed Applied Water Science field study (Springer, 2025) on replacing flood irrigation of sugarcane with drip irrigation in Upper Egypt, which reports water-use efficiency +44%, sugarcane yield +22% and net profit +50%. That is an irrigation-technology intervention, not a digital-agriculture intervention, so it sits on the wrong side of the construct: right outcome variable, wrong treatment. Conversely, the World Bank 2021 report and the CGSpace e-extension paper are on the right treatment (digital technologies / e-extension) but the retrieved text yields no realised yield or income outcome — consistent with the indicator census note that Egypt's existing level 3 rests on an evaluation measuring diffusion and adoption rather than yield or income. A T5 Exa library abstract of a quasi-experimental Upper Egypt extension study reports adoption (41.7%) for mobile advisory services but gives yield gains only for farmer field schools and demonstration plots; T5 material is in any case not admissible for a statistic.
8.12.defnote: The name's parenthetical fixes the outcome as yield or income, but Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation whose measured outcome is diffusion and adoption of digital tools, not yield or income.

A1-CAND-IRR.src: FAO AQUASTAT, Irrigation in Africa in figures – AQUASTAT Survey 2005, Country profile: Egypt
A1-CAND-IRR.note: Dated reference year (1997) from the 2005 AQUASTAT survey round; more recent AQUASTAT country data (2002, 2013/2016) report areas in hectares rather than a published percentage. Next level not proposed: Not applicable: this is a carried candidate indicator and proposed_level is withheld by design (0). The main evidentiary limitation is the age of the quoted percentage (1997) and the absence in the supplied pages of a recent, explicitly published equipped-share percentage from a T1/T2 publisher. The published figure is stated as 'percent of cropland irrigated' rather than the exact phrase 'cultivated area equipped for irrigation'. In the Egyptian case AQUASTAT treats these as coincident: the same source and the AQUASTAT country page report cultivated area (arable + permanent crops) of 3 422 178 ha in 2002 and area equipped for irrigation of 3 422 178 ha in 2002, and state that 'All the area equipped for irrigation was used for irrigation in year 2002', i.e. effectively 100 percent. The 2016 AQUASTAT profile revises cultivated area to 3 761 000 ha (2013) but no matching equipped-area percentage is given in the retrieved pages. A T5 market page (ReportLinker) shows 99.63 percent of cropland for 2023, but T5 material cannot be used for a statistic.
